clue.text: What sort of car is it here?

definitions.text: What sort of car is it here?

indicators.note: asking what sort of thing these words are invites a rearrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: A puzzled onlooker asks what kind of motor is parked on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What sort of' asks for the letters of CAR IS IT to be sorted anew; the answer then describes the clue itself, which mocks a car with a word it hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire mocks its target, and this clue is a little mockery whose letters make the adjective for such ridicule.

clue.text: They know all the answers!

parts.note: the phrase usually describes smug know-alls, but here it is literally those who hold the answer cards at a quiz

explanation.surface: A grumble about insufferable people who think they know everything.
explanation.definitionFit: The people running a quiz hold the answer sheet, so they literally know every answer.

clue.text: One way to call for spirits.

definitions.text: One way to call for spirits.

parts.words: One way to call for spirits.
parts.note: sounds like ordering drinks at a bar, but means summoning ghosts by invocation

explanation.surface: A drinker's tip on how to order whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: To call up or summon spirits of the dead is an old, rare verb from the Latin for calling out.

clue.text: Aid to beauty, not even skin deep.

definitions.meaning: a make-up product such as powder or lipstick
merely superficial, touching only the surface of things

explanation.definitionFit: Make-up is a beauty product, and anything purely for show is called superficial in the same word.

clue.text: He seems to be also a model of in a taxi.

annotationWithheld.clue: He seems to be also a model of in a taxi.

clue.text: As old as Iago was to Othello.

definitions.meaning: in Shakespeare Iago holds the rank of ensign or standard-bearer to Othello

explanation.definitionFit: The word means very old, and is also an obsolete word for an ensign, the rank Iago holds.

clue.text: What better hopes? (anag.)

indicators.note: the printed abbreviation for anagram tells the solver to rearrange the preceding words

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question about whether anything could be more promising.
explanation.walkthrough: The old-style '(anag.)' label is the indicator; the fifteen letters of WHAT BETTER HOPES rearrange to the phrase for those in authority, who are where one's best hopes lie.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the people in authority, the ones who decide and on whom hopes are pinned.

clue.text: One of those counter attractions perhaps.

definitions.text: One of those counter attractions perhaps.

parts.words: One of those counter attractions perhaps.
parts.note: counter-attractions are rival draws, but read literally this is an attractive person behind a pub counter

explanation.surface: A remark about rival entertainments competing for the public.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman serving behind a bar counter could be the pub's draw for customers.

clue.text: "They dined on and slices of quince." (E. Lear.)

definitions.text: "They dined on and slices of quince." (E. Lear.)

parts.words: "They dined on and slices of quince." (E. Lear.)
parts.note: a quotation from Lear's The Owl and the Pussy-cat with one word left out, to be filled in

explanation.surface: A line from Edward Lear's nonsense poem with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: Old puzzles printed a gap in a quotation for the answer to fill; here it is the food the owl and the cat ate at their wedding feast.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's line runs 'They dined on mince and slices of quince', so the gap takes the chopped-meat word.

clue.text: No need for " cave " now.

parts.note: cave is the Latin for beware, the warning a schoolboy lookout once called out

explanation.surface: Sounds like a remark that potholers need no cave.
explanation.walkthrough: British public-school slang used Latin 'cave' (beware) as a warning that a master was coming; once no one is near, the warning is unnecessary.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means nobody is watching and it is safe to go ahead, so no warning cry is needed.

clue.text: Run over again-—like the carter back Orient.

indicators.note: back signals that the word carter is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: taken as written; that the last letter of 'the' would also follow on when read backwards is a coincidence, since Orient supplies the final letter
the Orient is the East, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: A carter heading back east covers the same ground twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns CARTER into RETRAC; 'like the' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To go back over a route or the steps one took is to trace them again.

clue.text: The violin of romance.

indicators.note: of here says the violin is made out of the letters of romance, rearranged

explanation.surface: A romantic phrase about the instrument of love songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Old-style clue: 'of' is the only signal that the seven letters of ROMANCE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Violins made in the Italian city famed for Stradivari and Amati are named after that town.

clue.text: Such rich cole might turn out too waxy!

indicators.note: turn out suggests the words rich cole turning into a fresh arrangement of letters

explanation.surface: A cabbage dish that is too rich might be too greasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waxy' is old British slang for angry, not greasy; 'cole' is cabbage, adding to the kitchen misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Being quick to anger is a hot temper, and old British slang called an angry person waxy.

clue.text: Do listen!

parts.note: an imperative plea for someone to pay heed

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea to an inattentive person.
explanation.definitionFit: The imperative verb asks someone to pay heed, just as the plea does.

clue.text: It's a fatal holding in which one finds rents lag.

indicators.note: in which one finds says the words rents lag are to be found jumbled within the answer

explanation.surface: A wrestling hold where torn clothing slows a grappler down.
explanation.definitionFit: Choking someone to death by gripping the throat is a lethal hold.

annotationWithheld.clue: The confection would arrive quite well.

clue.text: The tongue of one who brings' the hands together.

definitions.meaning: the swinging striker inside a bell

definitions.text: one who brings' the hands together

explanation.definitionFit: A bell's striker is called by the same word as a person applauding with their palms.

clue.text: A sign of the passive.

parts.note: sounds like grammar, but means a mark of a sluggish, inactive temperament

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on how to spot the passive voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Sluggish inactivity, a tendency to stay at rest, marks a passive nature.

clue.text: An answer that must be emphasised.

definitions.text: An answer that must be emphasised.

parts.words: An answer that must be emphasised.
parts.note: describes an answer given with emphasis, and the answer is itself the word for that

explanation.surface: A teacher's instruction to stress a key point.
explanation.definitionFit: Something emphasised has stress laid on it.

clue.text: Style should be' visible in the adornment it lends one.

indicators.note: visible in says the letters can be seen inside the run of words the adornment it lends

explanation.surface: Fashion advice: good style shows in the finery it gives the wearer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Style' is a verb here, to give a title to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To style someone is to give them a name or title, for example styling a knight 'Sir'.

clue.text: As a lover's pinch, which hurts and is ."

definitions.text: As a lover's pinch, which hurts and is ."

parts.words: As a lover's pinch, which hurts and is ."
parts.note: Cleopatra's line on death in Antony and Cleopatra, with its last word left out to be filled in

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Cleopatra likening the stroke of death to a lover's pinch.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap ends Cleopatra's line 'The stroke of death is as a lover's pinch, which hurts, and is desired.'
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line ends with the word for longed for, completing the quotation.

clue.text: Hardly the type to set the table in a roar.

definitions.text: Hardly the type to set the table in a roar.

parts.words: Hardly the type to set the table in a roar.
parts.note: to set the table in a roar is Hamlet's phrase for making diners laugh, which a stern person would not do

explanation.surface: A remark about a dull dinner guest who never gets a laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: A stern, severe person is unlikely to make the dinner company laugh.

clue.text: They come after the gees!

parts.note: gees sounds like horses, but is the letter G, which in the alphabet is followed by H

explanation.surface: Sounds like grooms or hounds chasing horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gees' (gee-gees) suggests horses; it is the spelt-out name of the letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: The spelt-out names of the letter H follow the letter G in the alphabet.

clue.text: Good man to tear about at any time.

indicators.note: about says the word for tearing goes round the outside of the other piece

parts.note: to rend is to tear apart

explanation.surface: A good man who would rip things apart whenever he likes.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman carries the courtesy title for one deserving reverence, a good man of the church.
